column5: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
column6: The earlier part of the Ps 95 sequence calls the worshiping community God's pasture-people and sheep of God's hand. It supplies the flock-and-owner setting that precedes the later verses on erring hearts, unknown ways, and wrath.

column5: prayer to be taught God's ways
column6: The commentary is itself a plea to be led along a defined road. Ps 25 asks God to make known God's ways and teach the psalmist God's paths, a direct Hebrew prayer parallel to the request for guidance.

column5: level path amid those lying in wait
column6: The commentary includes a road vulnerable to an ambush and distinguishes upright travel from being made to stray. Ps 27 asks to be taught God's way and led on a level path specifically because of hostile watchers.

column5: blind travelers led on unknown paths
column6: The prose treats a route as something found by marks and a traveler as liable to lose it. Isaiah promises to lead blind people by paths they do not know and to turn darkness to light and crooked ground straight before them.

column5: forsaking a way and returning for mercy
column6: The commentary makes the lost condition recoverable through a change of walking and repentance. Isaiah commands the wicked to forsake their way and return to the Lord, whose mercy and pardon answer that turn.

column5: walking in stubborn counsel and going backward
column6: The commentary contrasts the forward trace of guided people with following one's own desire or misleading predecessors. Jeremiah says the people walked in the counsels of their stubborn evil heart and went backward rather than forward.

column5: return and gathering after dispersion
column6: The commentary sets a united company on one route against dispersal from it. Deuteronomy describes God restoring the fortunes of a returning people and gathering them from the peoples among whom they have been scattered.

column5: water for a congregation and its livestock
column6: The commentary's journey imagery joins a guide, water, and a flock or herd. At Meribah Moses is told that water will come from the rock for the assembled community and its animals, a wilderness provision scene with both elements.

column5: walking in wicked counsel
column6: The commentary warns that a track may be defined by the wrong companions and ancestors. Ps 1 locates the blessed person's first refusal in not walking in the counsel of the wicked, before its standing and sitting images of belonging.

column5: guiding feet into the way of peace
column6: The commentary repeatedly locates guidance in actual feet and a road rather than an abstract orientation. Zechariah's hymn asks for light that will guide human feet into the way of peace.

column5: walking in darkness without knowing one's destination
column6: The commentary distinguishes a traveler carried toward a destination from one who has lost direction. Jesus warns that the person who walks in darkness does not know where he is going, a sharply corresponding formulation.

column5: blind guides and a shared fall
column6: The commentary makes the identity of the guide decisive and notices sight as necessary for finding the route. Jesus calls the Pharisees blind guides; when blind lead blind, both fall into a pit.

column5: sheep refuse an unknown voice
column6: The page's flock is safe only when it knows its guide rather than following every track. In the continuation of the shepherd image, sheep flee rather than follow a stranger because they do not know that voice.

column5: former branches broken off and present standing by faith
column6: The commentary argues that a community can pass from favor into judgment rather than carrying favor as descent. Paul says that some branches were broken off through unbelief and that the present reader stands only by faith.

column5: former branches can be grafted in again
column6: The commentary's movement from wrath through repentance to renewed guidance has a structural counterpart in Paul's claim that excluded branches can be grafted in again if they do not persist in unbelief.

column5: seed must die before it comes to life
column6: The commentary's two forms of disappearance ask whether entry into earth means extinction or a directed transformation. Paul's seed image says what is sown does not come to life unless it dies, giving burial-like loss a generative end.

column5: bad company corrupts good character
column6: The commentary's bad companion can divert a traveler after guidance has been received. Paul makes the same social mechanism explicit by warning that bad associations corrupt good character.

column5: forsaking the straight way and following Balaam
column6: The commentary joins departure from a straight track to imitation of a misleading predecessor. Second Peter says false teachers have forsaken the straight way, gone astray, and followed Balaam's way.

column5: straight paths for feet that heal the lame
column6: The commentary's road is not merely a verdict but a route that can steady or lose a walker. Hebrews asks the community to make straight paths for its feet so that what is lame is healed rather than dislocated.

column5: cling to a good way and avoid an evil one
column6: The commentary examines right paths, false companions, and distinct negative routes. Avot records a debate over the good way to which a person should cleave and the evil way from which one should keep distance, including good and evil friends among the answers.

column5: distance from a bad neighbor and the wicked
column6: The commentary's companion may either sustain the route or lead one away from it. Avot instructs its reader to keep far from a bad neighbor and not join the wicked, a rabbinic social safeguard for the path.

column5: one is led in the way one chooses
column6: The commentary differentiates God's bestowal of guidance from the traveler's active straying. Makkot crystallizes that tension in its maxim that a person is led along the way that person wants to go.

column5: prayer that ways be made straight
column6: Tobit's fatherly instruction combines fidelity, wise counsel, and a prayer that the son's ways be made straight and his paths prosper. It is a Jewish family-to-traveler counterpart to the commentary's route that must be walked rather than merely inherited.
